core.p: Compare how anger is presented in **A Poison Tree** and one other poem from the Conflict anthology. In your answer, you should consider the poets’ use of language, form and structure, and the influence of the contexts in which the poems were written. (20 marks)

bullets: Similarity: first-person speakers, simple song-like forms, natural and biblical imagery, revenge endings.
Difference: Blake’s allegory warns against hidden anger; Rossetti’s monologue invites sympathy for justified anger against social injustice.
core.p: Hinge: **concealed vs voiced anger**. Blake’s speaker hides his anger until it kills; Rossetti’s speaker, silenced by society, finally voices hers. Both draw on Eden imagery and both end in a kind of revenge.

plan: Imagery: tree and apple vs dove, dust and gold
Form and structure: allegorical couplets vs ballad with changing addressee
essays.q: Compare how anger is presented in A Poison Tree and one other poem.
essays.t: Model essay: A Poison Tree and Cousin Kate
essays.text:
Both Blake and Rossetti trace anger from an injury to an act of revenge; however, Blake presents anger that is deliberately concealed and morally corrupting, while Rossetti presents anger that society has forced into silence and that is finally, defiantly spoken.

The origins of the anger reveal the poets’ different attitudes. Blake’s first stanza is built on antithesis: ‘I was angry with my friend’ is balanced against ‘I was angry with my foe’, and the healthy choice, ‘I told my wrath, my wrath did end’, is set against the dangerous one, ‘I told it not, my wrath did grow.’ The anger itself is not the problem; the decision to hide it is. Rossetti’s speaker has no such choice. Her anger comes from injustice: a ‘great lord’ ‘lured’ her to his palace, ‘wore’ her ‘like a silken knot’ and ‘changed’ her ‘like a glove’, similes that reduce her to a fashion accessory to be discarded. The active verbs all belong to the lord, so her anger is a response to powerlessness. Where Blake’s speaker is responsible for his anger, Rossetti’s is a victim of someone else’s power.

Both poets use nature and the Bible to explore how anger corrupts innocence. Blake’s extended metaphor shows the speaker tending his anger like a gardener: he ‘watered it in fears’ and ‘sunned it with smiles’, until it ‘bore an apple bright’. The allusion to the forbidden fruit of Genesis casts the speaker as the tempter, and the sibilance of ‘soft deceitful wiles’ suggests the serpent. Rossetti also draws on this imagery. Her speaker, once a ‘cottage maiden’, is now ‘an unclean thing, / Who might have been a dove’; the dove, a symbol of purity and the Holy Spirit, measures what she has lost. Her antithesis, ‘I sit and howl in dust, / You sit in gold and sing’, places her among the fallen in the dust of Genesis while Kate is raised ‘on high’. Both poets thus present anger as part of a fall from innocence, but Blake’s speaker falls through his own deceit, while Rossetti’s was pushed.

The forms reflect these differences. Blake’s four quatrains of rhyming couplets, in a sing-song trochaic rhythm, sound like a nursery rhyme or a parable; the cheerful form makes the sinister content more chilling, and nine lines beginning with ‘And’ make the growth of the anger feel unstoppable. Rossetti’s ballad stanzas are also regular, but the poem is structured by a change of addressee that charts her rising anger: she speaks first to the reader in lament, then turns on ‘Lady Kate, my cousin Kate’ with sarcasm, and finally declares that she ‘would have spit into his face’, a shockingly unladylike image for a Victorian woman’s voice. Blake’s anger stays hidden behind smiles until the end; Rossetti’s becomes louder with every stanza.

The endings complete each poem’s argument. Blake’s speaker finds his foe ‘outstretched beneath the tree’, and the shift to the present tense, ‘In the morning glad I see’, together with the single word ‘glad’, reveals a man so corrupted that murder brings joy. Writing in Songs of Experience, Blake, who attacked a Church that taught people to repress feeling, warns that suppressed anger becomes sin. Rossetti’s volta, ‘Yet I’ve a gift you have not got’, turns to the speaker’s son, ‘my shame, my pride’, whom the childless lord ‘would give lands’ to have as an heir. Her revenge is not murder but the knowledge of his loss. Rossetti, who worked with ‘fallen women’ at a Highgate refuge, gives one of them the voice that Victorian society denied her. Ultimately, Blake asks us to condemn the speaker’s secret anger, whereas Rossetti asks us to understand the speaker’s open anger: for Blake the danger is silence, but for Rossetti silence is the injustice.
essays.thesis: Both Blake and Rossetti show anger growing from betrayal into revenge, but Blake presents anger that is deliberately concealed and morally corrupting, while Rossetti presents anger that has been forced into silence by society and is finally, defiantly spoken.
why: **AO2**: antithesis, verbs, similes, extended metaphor, allusion, sibilance, symbol, form, anaphora, change of addressee, tense shift, volta.
**Comparison**: concealment vs voice, sustained to the final sentence.
**AO3**: Songs of Experience and the Church; fallen women and Rossetti’s refuge work.

mistakes.r: Only Blake’s speaker causes a death; Rossetti’s revenge is emotional and dynastic.
The lord and society are blamed too; Kate may also be trapped (‘bound… with his ring’).
